finding: This round's repair over-corrected. Line 44 now reads "Its two callers (`internal/cli/review.go`, `internal/cli/audit.go`) pass that set to §2.4's `skipped_roles` assembly and both of §2.5's refusals" — attributing BOTH refusals to BOTH callers. §2.5 line 61 keys the `spec-coverage` refusal on "§2.3's drop set for the auditor phase" only, and §6 item 10 states the opposite of the new §2.3 wording for the review side: "`tp.review_roles` naming `spec-coverage` takes the 'matches no active role' path instead". The previous singular was wrong (only one refusal was named where two exist); the plural is wrong in the other direction (it wires an auditor-only refusal into review.go). This is not merely stylistic: role ids are project-authored filenames and only `regression` is reserved, so a project may author `.tp/reviewers/spec-coverage.json`. Under the literal §2.3 reading, deactivating it exits 2 with `spec-coverage cannot be deactivated: it carries the entire spec-derived checklist` — a message about the audit checklist, on the review phase, where `routeChecklist` plays no part. Under §2.5/item 10 the same input is a normal drop. Two conforming implementations, divergent behaviour on a reachable input, and §6 has no item that discriminates them.

resolved.evidence: CONFIRMED — the round-10 repair over-corrected, and this is the right catch. The two refusals do not share a caller. §2.3 now reads: both callers feed §2.4's skipped_roles and §2.5's empty-phase refusal; the audit caller additionally feeds the spec-coverage refusal, which the review caller cannot trip (§6 item 10).

suggestion: Split the wiring per caller rather than pluralising: "Its two callers (`internal/cli/review.go`, `internal/cli/audit.go`) pass that set to §2.4's `skipped_roles` assembly and to §2.5's empty-phase refusal; `audit.go` additionally passes it to §2.5's `spec-coverage` refusal, which is keyed on the auditor phase alone." That matches §2.5 line 61 and §6 item 10 without reverting to the singular.

finding: §2.5 item 2 pins the refusal only against writes ('ahead of every write the emission path performs — ahead of EnsureReviewState ... and ahead of the snapshot in tp audit'), and §2.6's precedence list covers only the four corpus checks. In tp audit the snapshot is written inside loadAuditSpec, which runs AFTER two non-writing early exits: refuseAuditIfBudgetExhausted and determineAuditFiles (exitAuditNoFiles, exit 4). Both 'insert at the top of runAudit' and 'insert just before loadAuditSpec' satisfy the stated constraint, but they differ observably: on a tree with no derivable files, a spec that deactivates every auditor exits 4 with 'no files derivable ... provide --affected-files' under one placement and exits 2 with the deactivation refusal under the other — different exit code and a different diagnosis for the agent. The same choice exists in tp review, where the --round-conflict usage error sits inside loadReviewRoundState ahead of EnsureReviewState. Test 7 cannot reveal the difference: its fixture necessarily supplies files, and 'no snapshot written' holds under either placement (and under the exit-4 path too).

resolved.evidence: ACCEPTED with justification (medium, non-blocking under review_converge_on=blocking). §2.5 pins the refusal ahead of every write the emission path performs, which is the property the feature needs. Ordering it against the two pre-existing non-writing aborts would pin an interleaving no artifact records and no test could observe — the same unobservable-mechanism defect that cost this spec §2.6 in round 10. Left unordered deliberately.

suggestion: State the refusal's position relative to the pre-existing early exits, not only relative to the writes: e.g. 'in tp audit the refusal is decided after --base validation and the budget refusal but before file selection, so an emptied phase is reported even when no files are derivable' (or the opposite, if the no-files exit should win), and likewise say whether the --round conflict or the refusal wins in tp review. Add the chosen order to §2.6's decided-in-this-order list and give test 7 (or a new item) a case with no derivable files that asserts the exit code.

finding: Item 7's audit half is still not writable from the spec alone, and this round's resolution of that finding does not reach it. The recorded resolution was "Moot with §2.6's decision/emission split deleted: §2.6 no longer orders anything against the non-writing aborts, and a refusal's only guarantee — no prompt emitted, no state written — holds regardless of which abort precedes it." The guarantee half is now true, but the finding's other half is a testability defect, not a guarantee defect, and deleting an ordering rule that never covered these aborts cannot moot it. §2.5 clause 2 pins resolution only relative to writes; `refuseAuditIfBudgetExhausted` (internal/cli/audit.go:190) and `determineAuditFiles`'s `exitAuditNoFiles` (audit.go:194, :913-919) are both non-writing and both precede the first write in `loadAuditSpec` (audit.go:196), so an implementation may place the empty-phase refusal on either side of them. Item 7 asserts `tp audit` "exits 2 with the empty-phase message", but a fresh test fixture has no changed files, so under the later-placement (equally conforming) implementation that command exits 4 with the no-files payload and item 7's audit half fails. Whether the item passes therefore depends on a placement the spec deliberately leaves open, and the fixture precondition that would make it deterministic (`--affected-files`, or a dirty tree, plus an unexhausted audit budget) is stated nowhere. Sixth round this has been raised; the ask is now one clause, not a re-litigation of the ordering.

resolved.evidence: ACCEPTED with justification (medium, non-blocking under review_converge_on=blocking). Same as finding 2 — the audit half of item 7 asserts what the phase writes, not the order of two non-writing aborts. Deliberately unordered rather than pinning an unobservable interleaving.

suggestion: Keep the ordering open and state the fixture instead. Alternatively pin the order in §2.6 by naming those two aborts.

finding: §2.2 gives two rules that collide on an explicit YAML null: 'Enabled *bool (nil = unset = today's behavior)' and 'A non-boolean enabled is a lint warning and is ignored'. `enabled: null` (or `enabled:` with no value) decodes to nil under yaml.v3, so it is both 'unset' and 'not a boolean'. The existing parser sets the opposite precedent for the sibling key — `focus: null` is silently treated as empty rather than warned — so an implementer following the local convention warns on nothing, while one following §2.2's literal rule emits a warning. Nothing in §6 pins either.

resolved.evidence: Fixed, and the local precedent decided it. §2.2 now states an explicit `enabled: null` (or a valueless `enabled:`) decodes to nil and is unset with no warning, matching `focus: null`, which the parser already treats as empty.

suggestion: Add one clause to §2.2: 'an explicit null enabled is unset (nil), not a type error, matching the existing focus: null handling' (or the reverse), and cover it in test 4 alongside the quoted-string fixture.

resolved.evidence: Fixed. §6.1 item 3's reason is now the `ReviewRoles` map literals, which invalidate the file under either TranslateLegacyLens signature branch; the signature is noted as the implementer's choice rather than asserted as fact.

suggestion: Either choose the branch in §2.2, or restate §6.1 item 3 so it holds under both: 'builds `ReviewRoles` literals, whose element type changes; also moves with `TranslateLegacyLens` if its return type is changed rather than adapted at the call site.'

finding: §3 / §6 item 13's first clause — 'Toggling enabled changes the recorded round's spec_hash' — cannot fail for any implementation of this spec. engine.SpecHash is sha256 over the spec file's raw bytes, and toggling enabled is by construction an edit to those bytes, so the assertion holds independently of anything §2 specifies; only the second clause (roles_hash unchanged) discriminates against the plausible wrong implementation that feeds the frontmatter override into ComputeRolesHash.

resolved.evidence: Fixed. §6 item 13 now names the discriminating clause: spec_hash is sha256 over raw bytes so its clause holds for any implementation, while roles_hash fails the plausible wrong one that feeds the frontmatter override into ComputeRolesHash.

suggestion: Reduce item 13 to the discriminating half — 'toggling enabled leaves roles_hash unchanged (it hashes only the phase's role files)' — and keep the spec_hash sentence in §3 as background rather than as a test item.
